solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: GB due, amazingly, to do software fix

indicators.note: amazingly suggests the letters of GB due have been thrown into a surprising new order

explanation.surface: Someone is told that, astonishingly, Great Britain has to sort out some faulty computer code.
explanation.walkthrough: 'amazingly' rearranges the letters of GB DUE.
explanation.definitionFit: Programmers remove errors, or bugs, from code; the verb for that repair work is this one.

clue.text: Blue feathers getting tossed

parts.note: down is the soft fine feathering of birds
to cast is to throw or toss, and the past form matches

explanation.surface: A sad scene of a bird's plumage being thrown about.
explanation.definitionFit: Feeling blue means feeling low and dejected, a synonym for being gloomy in spirit.

clue.text: River coming away from sunny bay

indicators.note: coming away from says one piece is detached and removed from the other word

parts.note: a sunny day is a bright one

explanation.surface: A river flows out of a sun-drenched bay.
explanation.walkthrough: 'coming away from' removes R from BRIGHT.
explanation.definitionFit: A bight is a wide curving bay or indentation in a coastline, as in the Great Australian one.

clue.text: Piano's not entirely inadequate, winning all the trophies

parts.note: a grand is a grand piano, and the 's adds an S

indicators.note: not entirely means the word loses its final letter, so it is incomplete

parts.note: a lame excuse is a weak, inadequate one

explanation.surface: A pianist who swept every prize is being told the playing was nevertheless somewhat poor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not entirely' trims the E off LAME, leaving LAM.
explanation.definitionFit: In tennis and other sports a clean sweep of all the major championships in a season earns this title.

clue.text: Very good to interrupt boss — or foolish

indicators.note: to interrupt means one piece breaks into the middle of the other

parts.note: a boss is a raised knob or stud on a surface such as a shield
PI, short for pious, is the crossword stand-in for very good

explanation.surface: An employee weighs whether cutting in on the manager is wonderful or daft.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to interrupt' signals the insertion. A boss here is an ornamental knob, not a manager; 'Very good' is the crossword convention for pious.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words describe someone lacking good sense, so they are straightforward synonyms.

clue.text: Hint that's a lot of rubbish?

definitions.meaning: a hint or useful pointer, such as advice on a horse
a rubbish dump in British usage, a lot (plot of land) full of waste

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a suggestion is worthless nonsense.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a lot' plays on a lot as a plot of land; British speakers call a refuse dump by this name.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses are standard: a useful pointer, and in British English a place where waste is dumped.

clue.text: Dangerous fish? Greek character fled, with cry of surprise

parts.note: pi is a letter of the Greek alphabet
ran away is to have fled
ha is an exclamation of surprise

explanation.surface: A Greek man ran off shouting in alarm, perhaps at a dangerous fish.
explanation.definitionFit: This South American freshwater species is notorious for its razor teeth and feeding frenzies.

clue.text: Course in Oxford is hard

indicators.note: in tells us the letters sit inside the words that follow, spanning their boundaries

explanation.surface: A student finds an Oxford degree course tough going.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' points to letters hidden across oxforD IS Hard. The academic sense of 'Course' is the false trail; it is a course of a meal.
explanation.definitionFit: A dish is one part of a meal, such as a main course or a pudding served on a plate.

clue.text: Dicey moment if heads of finance house are discovered in error

indicators.note: are discovered in says these pieces are found placed within the other word

parts.note: a clanger is British slang for an embarrassing blunder or mistake

indicators.note: heads of means the first letter of each of the following words

explanation.surface: A tense moment arises when the leaders of a financial firm are caught out making a mistake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'heads of' and 'are discovered in' signal the pick and the insertion. Dropping a clanger is British slang for making an embarrassing blunder.
explanation.definitionFit: A situation of suspense whose outcome is uncertain, named after serials ending with heroes dangling from heights.

clue.text: Carry on endlessly with dog to get bird

indicators.note: endlessly means the last letter is cut off

parts.note: to wage a war or campaign is to carry it on
to dog someone is to follow or tail them

explanation.surface: Someone keeps going on and on, following a dog, to reach a bird.
explanation.walkthrough: 'endlessly' cuts the last letter. 'dog' is a verb meaning follow, not the animal.
explanation.definitionFit: This small songbird is named for its constantly bobbing tail and is common by British streams.

clue.text: Husband leaving local church area for capital city

indicators.note: leaving says this letter departs from the longer word

parts.note: a parish is the district served by a local church

explanation.surface: A husband abandons his home parish for the big city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'leaving' removes H from PARISH.
explanation.definitionFit: The French capital on the Seine is the city meant here.

clue.text: Share of proceeds is not entirely attractive

indicators.note: not entirely means the word is incomplete, losing its last letter

parts.note: cute means attractive or pretty

explanation.surface: Someone grumbles that their portion of the takings is not quite appealing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not entirely' removes the final E of CUTE.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone's portion of profits or loot is commonly called their slice or share.

clue.text: Clearing out records, as it might be, is corrupting

definitions.text: Clearing out records, as it might be
definitions.meaning: read whimsically as ..., taking documents out of files

explanation.surface: Purging the archives is said to be a corrupting act.
explanation.walkthrough: 'as it might be' admits the first sense is invented: DE- (removing) plus FILING (records).
explanation.definitionFit: To defile is to pollute or sully, so the participle matches 'corrupting' as a synonym.

clue.text: Science centre heading off effective classifying

parts.note: a lab, short for laboratory, is a centre for science

indicators.note: heading off means the first letter is removed

parts.note: a telling argument is an effective one

explanation.surface: A research centre moves away from effective sorting methods.
explanation.walkthrough: 'heading off' removes the T of TELLING, leaving ELLING.
explanation.definitionFit: Attaching tags or names to things sorts them into categories, which is the sense of classifying.

clue.text: Dangerous material? Most suitable to engage in a plea for help

indicators.note: to engage in means one piece is drawn inside the other

parts.note: SOS is the international distress signal
best means most suitable or fitting

explanation.surface: A worker asks which hazardous substance is the right one for an emergency call.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to engage in' signals the insertion; the question mark flags the definition as an example of dangerous material.
explanation.definitionFit: This fibrous mineral was once used for insulation but its fibres are now known to cause lung disease.

clue.text: Tell everything about the accident in the coffee-house?

definitions.meaning: to reveal a secret in full
literally knocking over coffee beans in a café

explanation.surface: Someone reports on a mishap at a café.
explanation.walkthrough: The idiom for revealing secrets is read literally: in a coffee-house the beans really could get knocked over.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means disclosing secret information, confessing all.

clue.text: Repeat it before scoundrel appears in middle of week

indicators.note: before places the first piece ahead of what follows
appears in says one piece shows up inside the other
middle of takes the central letters of the word

parts.note: a rat is a contemptible, treacherous person

explanation.surface: An instruction to say something again before a villain turns up on Wednesday.
explanation.walkthrough: 'middle of' takes the two central letters of 'week'; 'appears in' signals the insertion.
explanation.definitionFit: To do or say something again and again is a synonym for repeating it.

clue.text: Last tramline is buckled

indicators.note: buckled rails are twisted out of shape, so the letters are bent into a new order

explanation.surface: The final stretch of tram track has bent out of shape.
explanation.walkthrough: 'is buckled' rearranges TRAMLINE.
explanation.definitionFit: Something terminal is final, coming at the very end, as in a terminal illness or station.

clue.text: Dessert that is served after last of soup

indicators.note: served after places this piece behind the one before it
last of takes the final letter of the following word

parts.note: IE abbreviates id est, Latin for that is

explanation.surface: A pudding is brought out once the soup is finished.
explanation.walkthrough: 'last of' gives P from SOUP; 'served after' puts IE behind it.
explanation.definitionFit: A baked pastry with sweet filling, such as apple, is served as a pudding course.

clue.text: Eg two or three runs I'm to get in physical exercise

indicators.note: to get in means these pieces are placed inside the other

parts.note: PE is physical education, school exercise lessons
R is the cricket abbreviation for runs

explanation.surface: A runner counts a couple of laps during a gym class.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to get in' signals the insertion. 'Eg' marks two and three as examples of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Two and three are examples of numbers divisible only by one and themselves.

clue.text: Girl showing style, not the first

indicators.note: not the first means the opening letter is dropped

parts.note: class is style or elegance, as in she has class

explanation.surface: A young woman shows flair, though not the winning sort.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not the first' removes the C of CLASS.
explanation.definitionFit: A Scottish and northern English word for a young woman, now common everywhere.

clue.text: Expect article will be penned by a comedian

indicators.note: will be penned by means enclosed, as in a pen, by the following piece

parts.note: a wit is a clever, funny person
a is the indefinite article

explanation.surface: Someone anticipates a piece of writing from a funny person.
explanation.walkthrough: 'will be penned by' puts A inside WIT. The writing sense of 'penned' is the decoy.
explanation.definitionFit: To wait for something is to look forward to it, synonymous with expecting it.

clue.text: Best spinner

explanation.walkthrough: 'spinner' suggests a cricket bowler, but here it is the toy.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses are standard: supreme in rank, and a child's whirling toy.

clue.text: English literature is initially terribly highbrow?

indicators.note: initially takes the first letter of the following word

explanation.surface: Someone remarks that studying English literature seems dreadfully lofty at first.
explanation.walkthrough: 'initially' gives T from TERRIBLY. The question mark admits that highbrow and elitist are only loosely equivalent.
explanation.definitionFit: Highbrow tastes are those of an intellectual elite, so snobbish favouring of the few fits.

clue.text: Dozy agent surrounding sheltered area

indicators.note: surrounding means the first piece wraps around the other

parts.note: a spy is a secret agent
the lee is the side sheltered from the wind

explanation.surface: A drowsy secret agent lurks around a sheltered spot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'surrounding' signals the agent wrapping around the sheltered area.
explanation.definitionFit: Dozy describes someone drowsy and half asleep, a straightforward synonym.

clue.text: Hotel residents having no time for estimate

indicators.note: having no says this letter is missing from the word

parts.note: people staying at a hotel are its guests

explanation.surface: Busy hotel visitors have no time to give a rough figure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'having no' removes one T from GUESTS.
explanation.definitionFit: A rough calculation or approximation is a synonym for a guess as a noun.
